Test differences in forecast accuracy between models (Diebold-Mariano)

Source: R/eval-dm.R
mt_dm_test.Rd

Tests whether models of a backtest differ in their expected score with the Diebold-Mariano test (Diebold and Mariano 1995). By default the long-run variance is the equal-weighted cosine (EWC) estimate with fixed-smoothing critical values from a t distribution, as Lazarus, Lewis, Stock and Watson (2018) recommend for tests of a single restriction; the Diebold-Mariano statistic is such a test, of the mean loss difference. The fixed-smoothing test of Coroneo and Iacone (2020) for the Diebold-Mariano test, with a Daniell-kernel periodogram estimate, and the version of forecast::dm.test(), with the small-sample correction of Harvey, Leybourne and Newbold (1997), are options. It complements mt_score_table(), which shows the mean scores: the test says whether a difference is larger than the variation between forecast origins.

Usage

mt_dm_test(
  backtest,
  ref = NULL,
  metrics = "crps",
  targets = NULL,
  by = NULL,
  alternative = c("two.sided", "less", "greater"),
  varestimator = c("ewc", "daniell", "acf", "bartlett")
)

Arguments

backtest

An mt_backtest() or mt_compare() result with at least two models. Models are identified by model, and by "model (prep)" when a model was backtested with several preprocessing pipelines.

ref

Reference model (default: the first model). Every other model is compared with it.

metrics

Scores to compare: "crps", "wis", "ae" (absolute error of the median) and "se" (squared error of the median). CRPS and WIS compare whole predictive distributions; "ae" and "se" the medians only.

targets

Targets to test (default: all in the backtest; see quantities and contrast in mt_backtest()).

by

Optional stratum columns (for example "sex"): the losses per origin and the tests are then computed separately for each of their values.

alternative

"two.sided", "less" (the model has a lower expected score than ref, that is, it is more accurate) or "greater".

varestimator

"ewc" (equal-weighted cosine estimate with fixed-smoothing t critical values, default), "daniell" (Daniell-kernel periodogram estimate with fixed-smoothing t critical values, Coroneo and Iacone 2020), "acf" (sum of the autocovariances, as forecast::dm.test()) or "bartlett" (Bartlett weights, as forecast::dm.test()). See Variance estimators.

Value

A data.table with one row per model (other than ref), value of by, target, metric and horizon: model, ref, the by columns, target, metric, horizon (a factor: the horizons, then "all"), n_origins (number of losses tested), lag (largest autocovariance lag used; NA for "ewc" and "daniell"), df (degrees of freedom of the t distribution), score and score_ref (mean loss over the origins), mean_diff (score - score_ref; negative when the model is more accurate), statistic and p_value.

Details

The test uses one loss per forecast origin, the time index of a rolling-origin backtest. Scores of the cells of one origin and horizon (ages, strata) concern the same test year and are strongly dependent, so they are averaged first:

  • per horizon h: the mean score over the cells of each origin at that horizon gives one loss per origin and model. The differences between the losses of a model and of ref form a series over the origins. The errors of forecasts h years ahead from consecutive origins build up over overlapping years, so the differences are autocorrelated.

  • overall (horizon = "all"): the mean of these per-horizon losses over all horizons gives one loss per origin. Only origins scored at every horizon enter.

Only cells scored for both models enter (the same origin, horizon, stratum, age group, year and target). Scores are not negative, so the loss is the score itself.

Variance estimators

With d_t the loss differences of the T origins (t = 1, ..., T, in the order of the origins) and dbar their mean:

  • "ewc" (default): Lambda_j = sqrt(2 / T) * sum_t (d_t - dbar) * cos(pi * j * (t - 1/2) / T) for j = 1, ..., nu, the long-run variance Omega = mean(Lambda_j^2), the statistic sqrt(T) * dbar / sqrt(Omega) and p-values from the t distribution with nu degrees of freedom, nu = 0.4 * T^(2/3) cosine terms as Lazarus et al. (2018) recommend for the EWC test, rounded down and at least 1 (1 for up to 11 origins, 2 for 12 to 20, 3 for 21 to 31). There is no further small-sample correction. The estimate does not use the horizon, so there is a test for every horizon with at least 2 origins; lag is NA.

  • "daniell": the weighted periodogram estimate with the Daniell kernel of Coroneo and Iacone (2020, Eq. 8), Omega = (1 / m) * sum_j I_j for the first m Fourier frequencies lambda_j = 2 * pi * j / T, with I_j = |sum_t d_t exp(-i lambda_j t)|^2 / T, and p-values from the t distribution with 2 m degrees of freedom (their Eq. 9). m = floor(T^(1/3)), at least 1, as in their simulations and application (Section 5: the best combination of size and power in a preliminary study): 1 for up to 7 origins, 2 for 8 to 26. lag is NA. Coroneo and Iacone (2020) also propose the Bartlett-kernel estimate with bandwidth floor(T^(1/2)) and fixed-b critical values given as a polynomial for two quantiles, which give no p-values; it is not implemented. They do not use the equal-weighted cosine estimate.

  • "acf": the test of forecast::dm.test(e1, e2, h = h, power = 1) with e1 and e2 the losses per origin: the variance is the sum of the autocovariances up to lag h - 1, the statistic has the correction of Harvey et al. (1997), and p-values come from the t distribution with T - 1 degrees of freedom. With origins spaced s years apart (for example origins = seq(1981, 2001, by = 10)), test years overlap only up to lag ceiling(h / s) - 1, which is used instead; with unequal spacing the smallest gap counts. When T is not larger than the number of lags needed (T <= h for consecutive origins), or when the variance estimate is not positive, there is no test (statistic and p_value are NA, with a warning of class mt_warning_dm); forecast::dm.test() falls back to lag 0 in the second case, which rejects a true null hypothesis about half the time.

  • "bartlett": as "acf" with Bartlett weights 1 - k / h for the autocovariances at lags k = 1, ..., h - 1, as in forecast::dm.test().

Size and power with few origins

Backtests have few origins, and with consecutive origins the test years of horizons above 1 overlap. In a simulation under the null hypothesis (20,000 series of loss differences that are sums of h consecutive independent normal errors, a moving average of order h - 1 as for forecasts h years ahead from consecutive origins), the "acf" test at the nominal 5% level rejected in 10% (h = 2), 16% (h = 3) and 19% (h = 5) of the samples with 7 origins, and in 16% to 17% with 15 or 16 origins at h = 5; "bartlett" in 10% to 15% with 7 origins. Their p-values are too small with few overlapping origins. The fallback to lag 0 of forecast::dm.test(), needed in 4% of the samples with 7 origins at h = 3 and in 22% at h = 5, rejected in 39% to 55% of them, so that the test with the fallback rejected in 27% at h = 5 with 7 origins. The EWC test rejected in 4.9% to 7.2% of the samples with 7 origins and in 4.8% to 7.0% with 15 or 16 origins (h from 1 to 5). Its size is nearly correct, but with few origins it has few degrees of freedom and low power: with 7 origins (nu = 1) it finds only large and consistent differences. The "daniell" test of Coroneo and Iacone (2020) has more degrees of freedom (2 with 7 origins, 4 with 8 to 26) and rejected in 4.9%, 6.0%, 7.6%, 10.5% and 15.3% of the samples with 7 origins at h from 1 to 5, and in 4.8% to 13.8% with 15 or 16 origins: its size is close to 5% for h up to 2, where test years overlap little, and too large beyond. Coroneo and Iacone (2020) studied one-step forecasts with 40 or 120 origins. More origins, or origins spaced h years apart, which avoid overlapping test years, give more informative tests. The p-values are not adjusted for the number of tests (models, targets, horizons); see stats::p.adjust().

References

Coroneo L, Iacone F (2020). Comparing predictive accuracy in small samples using fixed-smoothing asymptotics. Journal of Applied Econometrics 35(4): 391-409. doi:10.1002/jae.2756

Diebold FX, Mariano RS (1995). Comparing predictive accuracy. Journal of Business & Economic Statistics 13(3): 253-263.

Harvey D, Leybourne S, Newbold P (1997). Testing the equality of prediction mean squared errors. International Journal of Forecasting 13(2): 281-291.

Lazarus E, Lewis DJ, Stock JH, Watson MW (2018). HAR inference: recommendations for practice. Journal of Business & Economic Statistics 36(4): 541-559.

See also

mt_compare(), mt_score_table(), mt_score().

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 1990:2012)
bt <- mt_compare(list(rw = rwd(), lc = lee_carter()), x, origins = 2001:2007, h = 3, n_draws = 30)
mt_dm_test(bt)
#>     model    ref target metric horizon n_origins   lag    df      score
#>    <char> <char> <char> <char>  <fctr>     <int> <int> <num>      <num>
#> 1:     lc     rw   rate   crps       1         7    NA     1 0.03593905
#> 2:     lc     rw   rate   crps       2         7    NA     1 0.03653935
#> 3:     lc     rw   rate   crps       3         7    NA     1 0.03743453
#> 4:     lc     rw   rate   crps     all         7    NA     1 0.03663764
#>     score_ref   mean_diff statistic    p_value
#>         <num>       <num>     <num>      <num>
#> 1: 0.04750121 -0.01156216 -4.218645 0.14817141
#> 2: 0.04969118 -0.01315182 -5.091841 0.12345620
#> 3: 0.05588227 -0.01844774 -6.541768 0.09656861
#> 4: 0.05102489 -0.01438724 -5.300051 0.11872013
# the version of forecast::dm.test()
mt_dm_test(bt, varestimator = "acf")
#>     model    ref target metric horizon n_origins   lag    df      score
#>    <char> <char> <char> <char>  <fctr>     <int> <int> <num>      <num>
